segments.say: Fifteen hotel guests poisoned by chlorine. The alarm ran on email.
segments.show: 15 guests at a hotel in Germany were poisoned by excessive chlorine after the alarm that emailed operators never went out (Security Affairs, 15 Nov).

segments.say: Microsoft's outage stopped the warning emails at a German hotel pool.
segments.show: Per Security Affairs, citing Notebookcheck and WDR: the sauna-area system at Hotel Ling Bao, Phantasialand (Brühl) emailed operators when chlorine rose too high. During Microsoft's 12-14 Nov outage, those emails didn't go out.

segments.say: Forty responders came. Four guests went to hospital.
segments.show: German emergency services sent 40 first responders; local media reported four people taken to hospital. The pool has since reopened.

segments.say: Myth: a cloud alert is a safety system. Give critical alarms an offline backup.
segments.show: Tom's Hardware, quoted by Security Affairs: architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that keeps working offline.
segments.card: Add a physical / offline backup alarm

Microsoft 365 outage, real-world harm: a German hotel's chlorine alarm emailed operators. During the 12-14 Nov outage the emails didn't go out and 15 guests were poisoned, Security Affairs reports. Safety alarms need an offline backup.

#Resilience #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
15 hotel guests poisoned by chlorine. The alarm ran on email. ☁️

What Security Affairs reported (15 Nov), citing Notebookcheck and WDR:
→ A sauna-area system at Hotel Ling Bao in Phantasialand, Brühl, emailed operators when chlorine got too high
→ During Microsoft's 12-14 Nov outage those emails didn't go out, and chlorine kept rising
→ 15 guests were affected; 40 first responders were sent and four people went to hospital, per local media
→ The pool was closed and has since reopened
→ The lesson: an alarm that depends on email fails when email fails

What to do: list every safety or security alert that only travels by email or one cloud service. Give the critical ones a physical or offline backup, and test it.

cover.hook: €805 million. For one default setting in Facebook's app.
cover.sub: Italy's privacy regulator says the Android app read users' photo galleries without specific consent.

slides.title: The feature
slides.body: "Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook", live since 2023, suggests photos and videos from your phone to post. Italy's Garante says the Android app accessed them and their metadata without specific consent.

slides.label: fine on Meta Platforms Ireland
slides.note: About 20 million Android users in Italy affected

slides.title: 3 problems
slides.body: One gallery permission covered several purposes. The notice ("enable other features") didn't say it also turned on gallery suggestions. And the feature was on by default.

slides.title: Meta's answer
slides.body: Meta told Reuters users must grant device permission first and can revoke it in settings. The Garante said Meta's changes came too late and only reached users who updated the app.

slides.title: Check your own app
items: List features that are on by default
Consent text that names the feature
Know what your app reads from the phone

items.x_text:
Meta fined €805M by Italy's Garante: the Facebook Android app's gallery-suggestions feature read photos, videos and metadata of ~20M users without specific consent, the regulator says. It was on by default. Meta has 60 days to fix it.

#Privacy #InfoSec
items.ig_caption:
€805 million. For one default setting in Facebook's app. 📸

What Security Affairs reported (15 Nov):
→ Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta Platforms Ireland €805 million
→ It says the Facebook Android app accessed photos, videos and their metadata without specific consent or proper information
→ The feature: "Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook", available since 2023, on by default
→ About 20 million Android users in Italy were affected
→ Meta told Reuters users must grant device permission first and can revoke it any time
→ Meta has 60 days to ask for separate, specific consent and keep the feature off by default

What to do: audit your own apps for features that are on by default, split permissions by purpose, and make consent text name the feature.

items.send_to: whoever approves your AI coding tools
items.x_text:
MCP servers in AI coding assistants: pinning the top-level package doesn't freeze its dependencies. A CSA note cites one commit-pinned server that ran 15 dependency sets in 5 weeks. Pin exact versions, use lockfiles, add release-age cooldowns.

#AISecurity #SupplyChain
items.ig_caption:
Your AI assistant's MCP server is "pinned". Its dependencies aren't. 🧩

What a Cloud Security Alliance note explained (15 Nov):
→ Red path: config says npx -y or uvx → the launcher resolves dependencies from a public registry on every launch → a new (possibly malicious) version can run without any config change
→ Corelight (cited by CSA) found 23 of 35 MCP servers install this way
→ One server pinned to a single commit ran with 15 different dependency sets over five weeks
→ Green path: exact versions + a committed lockfile or an image by digest + an internal, logged registry proxy = the same code every launch
→ CSA notes pinning also freezes vulnerable versions, so updates need a deliberate process

Defences: inventory every MCP server definition, pin exact versions, add release-age cooldowns, and review MCP config changes like code.

segments.say: Ten critical NetScaler flaws. One patch release.
segments.show: Citrix patched 28 NetScaler ADC and Gateway flaws, nine of them critical, plus a critical bug in NetScaler Console (SecurityWeek, 13 Nov).

segments.say: Nine are memory bugs in A D C and Gateway that can cause denial of service.
segments.show: Memory overflow bugs in packet processing, SMPP, DNS/DoH, NetScaler Push, Email OTP, EPA and ICA proxy can cause erroneous behaviour or DoS. Fixed in 14.1-73.57 and 13.1-64.39 and later.

segments.say: The tenth, in NetScaler Console, scores nine point four. No login needed.
segments.show: CVE-2026-120869 (CVSS 9.4) lets unauthenticated attackers bypass controls and reach restricted resources. All Console 14.1 builds before 14.1-74.34.

segments.say: Citrix reports no exploitation yet. Update to the fixed builds now.
segments.show: Citrix makes no mention of in-the-wild exploitation. It urges customers to update as soon as possible and lists preconditions per CVE in its advisory.
